chapter_theme: Songs at Thiruvannamalai (திருவருணை, 5 of 6): the poet confesses a counterfeit asceticism worn for gold, the trade of flattering patrons, and his bondage to courtesans who cheat and sell, sets out the diseased and maya-bound body, and asks for the feet, for release and for the gift of song; three love-laments in a woman's voice ask Murugan to come; the praise turns on the vel against Sura, Valli and Devayanai, and Murugan standing in the streets and at the tower of Arunai.
structure_note: Courtesan songs (429, 438, 439, 442), with 434 and 437 confessing a life spent on women;the false ascetic (428) and the flattering poet (436); the body and its diseases (433, 437, 441); love-laments in a woman's voice (430, 432, 440); the self-abuse litany (435); and pleas for song (431, 441).

428.reading: The poet confesses a counterfeit renunciation: head shaved, ochre cloth at the waist, matted hair grown and twisted, a tiger skin worn with flourish, tricks learned, penance known only as a word, ash smeared thick, while he stays caught in the net of the senses and wanders making gold; he asks Murugan to take a little notice of him as he wilts and in pity end his care. The praise names Murugan who cut down the tree in the sea, shattered the hill, entered the gods' world and took the hand of the elephant-reared bride, who came to Arunagiri and pities devotees who know, the son of Siva who bent the mountain and burned the cities with an idle laugh, and who entered the millet field in human form.
428.nuance: The plea is a confession, not a satire of others: the participles all lead to துவளும் எனை, 'me, who wilt'. He has worn both the shaved head (தலையை மழித்து) and the matted hair (சடையை வளர்த்து), every mark of the ascetic, and தவம் ஒரு சத்தத்து அறிந்து says he knew penance only as a sound. கனகம் இயற்றித் திரிந்து names the motive, gold. கொக்கு in the praise is taken as the mango tree that Sura became in the sea. சதிரொடு வப்ப and கதறு நிலைக்கைக்கு அமர்ந்த are obscure.

429.reading: The poet heaps abuse on courtesans: thieves who trade in their bodies, wicked and shameless, with bow-like brows and lifted breasts, who melt men's minds with laughter, frighten them with their eyes and fall on them, and who polish brass ornaments with ash to pass them off as gold; he asks to leave behind his delusion for them and bow single-minded at Murugan's golden feet. The praise is a battle scene in drum syllables, ghouls dancing with hands and drums and eating flesh as the demon armies fall to the vel, and ends with Guha who abides at Arunai.
429.nuance: திருட்டு வாணிப, 'thieving trade', names the commerce at once. பித்தளையில் பணி மிக நீறால் விளக்கியே குழையிட்ட புரட்டிகள்: the cheats wear brass ear-ornaments scoured with ash to shine like gold, so even their jewels deceive. ஒருமித்து, single-minded, is set against the divided heart the women produce.

430.reading: A love-lament for a girl: the speaker names what torments her, the flowers swarming with bees, the cool moonlight that burns like poison from a serpent's fang, and the arrows of Kama the warrior, and asks Murugan to come and embrace this girl filled with longing. The praise names Murugan the peacock hero honoured by Siva who bears a woman in his hair and by Vishnu, the bridegroom of the parrot raised by the elephant in Indra's city, who stands in the streets of Arunachala for the world to see, and who reduced Meru to dust and set the vel's mark on Brahma.
430.nuance: பூவையை நீ அணைக்க வரவேணும: the speaker asks the god to embrace the girl, so this is akam poetry in the voice of a mother or companion, not the poet's confession. The moon that burns is a classical torment of the lovesick. வாரணமான தத்தை is Devayanai, raised by Indra's elephant. The last line (நான்முகனார் பதத்தில் வேல் அடையாளம் இட்ட) is unclear: the vel's mark may be set on Brahma's feet or on his station.

431.reading: The poet asks that his heart not be lost to women with great breasts, that colic, fever, wind and bile and the other diseases not come near him, and that Death, the sinner, not come on his buffalo and throw the noose to seize him; he asks Murugan to pity this poet and give him songs of fine words fit for the learned. The praise names Murugan the Veda, bindu and nada, the true kadamba-wearer called Virabhadra and Kanda, the vel that split Meru, cut down Sura and pierced the sea, the lover of the golden girl of the hills, who sits in the beautiful tall tower of Sonagiri.
431.nuance: The three things the poet fears come in order, women, disease, Death, and the remedy is the gift of song (பாடல் மிக்க செஞ்சொல்), the poet asking to be made a poet. Murugan is given Siva's fierce name வீரபத்ர. கோபுரத்து அமர்ந்த places him at the temple tower of Arunai.

432.reading: A short song in a lovesick woman's voice: struck by Kama's flower arrows, by the cruel young moon spitting fire and by the cuckoo whose call destroys her modesty, she asks whether it is right that she waste away in longing. The praise names the chest that embraces the maiden of heaven, the hero whose anklets are fragrant with the gods' crowns, the bright vel standing at Arunai to be seen, and the Lord who breaks the back of Death.
432.nuance: நானும் மயலில் இளைக்கும் தரமோ: the woman speaks herself. நாணம் அழிய உரைக்கும் குயில்: the cuckoo's call makes her lose her shame. The last line, காலன் முதுகை விரிக்கும், gives Murugan a victory over Death even in a love song.

433.reading: In a rhythm of long vowels, the poet speaks of women whose speech is milk, honey and syrup, and of the body, a hut bound by the noose, made of skin, wind and flesh and stained, and asks whether he must tire and die of the unending disease of maya. The praise is a string of vocatives: Lord of the world, the high one, Veda, master, lord of the hill of light, way of jnana, king of the heavens, meaning of the many Vedas, vel-bearer, child, lord of the hunter girl, the support of the six centres, the hero.
433.nuance: The song is built of paired long syllables (ஞாலா மேலா வேதா போதா), so meaning bends to sound and several splits are guesses. மாயா ஓயா நோய், the never-ceasing disease of maya, makes maya itself the illness. சோதிக் கிரி is Arunachala, the hill of fire, and ஆறாதாரா names Murugan the six adharas of yoga.

434.reading: The poet says that much of his life has gone wandering in the net of women, and that now, knowing the praise the Vedas give Murugan, he will count his heart, gold, life and goods as Murugan's; to end this dog's sorrow he asks Murugan to come gladly on the peacock with his consorts, his six faces shining like the sun on a gem hill, praised by countless sages. The praise shows heavenly women chanting the Veda like cuckoos and parrots, drums sounding as the vel destroys the demons' army in the sea, and Murugan who married Hari's daughter and burns away the poet's trouble on the hill of Arunai.
434.nuance: அகம் பொன் ஆவி பொருள் என நினைந்து: the offering of heart, gold, life and goods is the gift of the whole self, the servant's surrender. அரிமகள், Hari's daughter, is Valli. The opening lines (பொறியுடல் இறந்து போனது அளவு ஏது) are hard to divide.

435.reading: The poet heaps names on himself: an outcast, futile, a doer of great sins, angry without patience, a fool, without renown, dark-natured, without understanding, blind, his senses running off, an unsteady clown, a spendthrift who gives nothing, a ruin of his line; he asks Murugan to come and grant that he think of the feet every day with a longing that never ends. The praise names Rama, who fought until Ravana's arms were broken and took back Sita, as his uncle, and Murugan who sent the vel to powder Meru and Sura, rode the peacock among the gods and dwells at Arunai.
435.nuance: கொடையிலாத ஊதாரி, a spendthrift who never gives, is a pointed paradox. The plea does not ask that desire end but that it turn: ஆசை வீடாமல், thinking of the feet with a longing that is not let go.

436.reading: The poet describes poets who, to end their poverty, liken rich men to the wish-granting tree, the rain cloud and Pari, praise them as fit to give heaps of gold at once, make 'thieving poems' of ornate figures to get money, and then spend what they earn on golden women and fall slaves in the net of their fish eyes; he asks whether one should come to that. The praise names Murugan sitting on the peacock at the northern side of the golden, jewelled tower of Arunai where Agama devotees and pure Vedic men gather, and the son of Siva who shares his left side with the peacock-like Uma, whose vel pierced Sura.
436.nuance: திருட்டுக் கவிகள்: the poet calls praise-poems for patrons theft, an unusual confession about his own craft; the patron comparisons (கற்பகம், புயல், பாரி) are the stock ones of court poetry. The money won by false praise ends with the courtesans, so the two trades are joined. The praise lines on the tower (உத்தர திக்கு, கலபக் கற்கி) are hard to construe.

437.reading: The poet tells how he was caught in the net of women whose eyes are likened to the deer, poison, the carp, Kama's arrow, the sea, the vel, the sword and the blue lily, and names the body as a poison of flesh, an oozing filth, a bloated corpse swinging with the three gunas, impermanent rubbish; he asks whether this delusion will ever clear. The praise names Rama, who struck Vali from behind a sal tree and gave Tara to Sugriva after Ravana had imprisoned Janaki in the grove of sorrow, as his uncle, and Murugan, son of the pure Lord of Sonagiri, whose kadamba-garlanded shoulders crushed the hill and who cut down Sura.
437.nuance: குணத்ரயத்தொடு தடுமாறும் ஊசல்: the body is a swing tossed by the three gunas. நித்தத்துவம் அற்ற செத்தை, 'rubbish without permanence'. The line உபாதியை ஒப்பித்துத் துனிப்பவத்து அற is obscure; உபாதி may be the limiting adjunct of philosophy or simply affliction.

438.reading: The poet lists the courtesans' kinds: those who flatter to the face, the scheming, the low-priced, the cunning, the deceitful in speech, those who for love of coin sell their breasts to many, who melt men with laughter and 'aha', thieves and forms of illusion; he asks when, leaving his revelling with them, he will reach the holy feet. The praise shows Siva dancing to drum syllables, worshipped by his devotees, Agastya, Vishnu, Brahma and the Goddess who nurtured dharma rejoicing in Murugan the eternal Lord who stands at Arunai, who smashed Sura and resettled the gods, the Lord of devotees.
438.nuance: காசாசையில் முலை பலர்க்கும் விற்பவர்: the song names the sale outright. அறம் வளர்த்த கற்பகம் is the Goddess as nurturer of dharma, rejoicing with the others in Murugan.

439.reading: The poet describes women with cloud-dark hair, bow brows, arrow eyes and breasts like Meru, who walk dancing down the good street crying the price of their breasts, lure those who come with deceitful play, and snatch their life with a powder of infatuation; he asks whether such women can be kin. The praise has drums sounding as the vel leaves Sura's thousand heads bare, shakes Meru and wrecks the demons' island; it names Murugan the son of Sivakami, the Shakti who is first, middle and cause of many things, and the one who rejoices at Arunachala in his love for Valli, daughter of Vishnu.
439.nuance: முலை விலைகூறி: the women cry their price in the street. மயல் தூள் மருத்திடு suggests a love-powder or drug given to the men. The string of Shakti's names (ஆதி மத்தி பலகாரணத்தி ... ஈசசத்தி) is hard to divide, and the phrase on Vishnu searching out the Veda for Brahma is tentative.

440.reading: A love-lament: the speaker names the roaring sea, darkened, its fishes stirred, and the moon that rises full of poison out of the mare-faced fire beneath the sea, and asks Murugan to think how to ease the infatuation of the girl with rain-dark hair and vine waist, and to come on the emerald peacock and give release. The praise names the chest that holds Valli's sandal-smeared breasts, the Lord of Indra's city, of Senthil and of Arunai, the vel that pierced the seven hills, and the one who ended the fear of the suns, Hari, Hara and Brahma.
440.nuance: The torments are the classical sea and moon, with the moon rising from வடவை, the submarine fire. முத்தி தரவேணும: the girl's longing is to be ended by mukti, so the akam frame opens onto the plea for release.

441.reading: The poet lists the diseases of his body, wind, bile, scrofula, abscess, dry colic, leprosy, chills, thirst, diabetes, the great belly, phlegm, vomiting, retention of urine and countless more, says he can no longer bear to carry it about the earth, and asks for the attainment of Siva-knowledge so that his tongue may praise the Thiruppugazh, full of Siva. The praise names Murugan the son of the coral-haired Siva who gave the blazing discus to Vishnu for his unfailing devotion, the vel that killed Sura, the hill, the lion-faced and the elephant-faced demons, and the Lord at Arunachala with the hunter girl and the elephant's daughter.
441.nuance: சிவமார் திருப்புகழை எனுநாவினில் புகழ: the book names itself, and the cure asked for is not health but the power to sing it. சிவஞான சித்தி joins knowledge and its attainment. The discus given to Vishnu for his devotion is told only as தொலையாத பத்தி.

442.reading: The poet speaks of women who, with eyes swift as Kama's arrows, chatter 'come, go' with the cunning of a hundred thousand minds, and of himself as a clown wholly in thrall to their musk-scented breasts, reviled by earth and sky, a fool without conduct, wretched and vile; he asks whether there will be a day when Murugan rules him among his devotees. The praise names the emerald Narayana, who embraced the sixteen thousand women of the northern cowherds, as his uncle, the ever-young king of Sonachala, and the lone vel thrown so the world might live, the sea dry and the demons fall as ash.
442.nuance: நூறாயிர மனமுடை, 'with a hundred thousand minds', is the women's fickleness. The poet asks to be ruled together with the devotees (அடியவரோடு), not alone. Krishna's sixteen thousand women stand in the praise just after the poet's own confession, without comment.

links.note: The Kural says neither the shaved head nor long matted hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; 428 confesses to both marks, the shaved head and the grown locks, with the condemned conduct, the hunt for gold, kept underneath.
Tirumular says the false garb is worn for the sake of eating; in 428 the poet confesses to wearing it to make gold, and asks for pity rather than claiming the garb.

Both list the same diseases (scrofula, the great belly, phlegm, colic, urinary flux). 243 asks that they not afflict him through his births; 441 gives up on the body and asks instead for Siva-knowledge and the power to sing the Thiruppugazh.

429 abuses the courtesans as cheats who scour brass ornaments with ash and wear them in their ears (பித்தளையிற் பணி மிக நீறால் விளக்கியே குழையிட்ட புரட்டிகள்). 1317 has the same picture, tarnished brass ornaments polished with ash to shine (மாசுற்றேறிய பித்தளையிற் பணி நீறிட்டே ஒளி பற்ற விளக்கிகள்). In both the false gold stands for the false love of a priced trade.

The Kural's man asks where she got this fire that burns when he moves away and is cool when he comes near (நீங்கின் தெறூஉம் குறுகுங்கால் தண்ணென்னும் தீ). 430's girl is burned by cool moonlight (சீதநிலா எறிக்கும் அனலாலே), and the cure asked is that the god come and embrace her. Both turn coolness and fire inside out in love-sickness, with nearness as the only cooling.

431 asks that diseases, colic, fever, wind and bile (சூலை வெப்பு அடர்ந்த வாத பித்தம்), not come near, and then asks for the gift of fine song (பாடல் மிக்க செஞ்சொல் தரவேணும்). 441 lists wind, bile, colic and many more, says it can no longer carry the body, and asks for the power to praise Thiruppugazh on its tongue (திருப்புகழை எனுநாவினிற் புகழ). In both songs the remedy asked for after disease is song itself.

The Kural says the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint bolted with the bar of shame (காமக் கணிச்சி உடைக்கும் நிறையென்னும் நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு). 432's woman says the cuckoo's call destroys her modesty (நாணம் அழிய உரைக்குங் குயிலாலே) as she wastes in longing. Both make shame the last barrier that love-sickness breaks.

The Naladiyar calls the body a paltry lodging (நொய்யதோர் புக்கில்) whose covering of skin, if torn, brings the crows. 433 names it a hut bound by the noose, made of skin, wind and flesh and stained (தோலாலே காலாலே ஊனாலே சூழ் பாசக் குடில் மாசு). Both set the body as a frail dwelling of skin against the sweet speech of women.

The Tirumanthiram tells how Nandi took body, wealth and life with water (உடல்பொருள் ஆவி உதகத்தாற் கொண்டு), the disciple's whole self given to the guru, and ended birth. 434 makes the same gift in its own words, counting heart, gold, life and goods as Murugan's (அகம் பொன் ஆவி பொருள் என நினைந்து). The pairing shows the song's offering as the old formula of surrender.

The Kural commands: cling to the clinging of the one without clinging, in order to let clinging go (பற்றுக பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை). 435, after heaping names on itself, does not ask that desire end but that he think of the feet daily with a longing not let go (நினது தாளை நாடோறு மனதில் ஆசை வீடாமல் நினையுமாறு). Both turn attachment toward the Lord instead of ending it.

436 describes poets who liken the rich to the kalpaka tree, the rain cloud and Pari and make thieving poems for money (திருட்டுக் கவிகள் பாடி). 271 renounces poets who liken base patrons to the pouring cloud and the wish-tree and who steal and twist old verses (பழைய மொழியைத் திருடி நெருடிக் கவிபாடி). Both name patron-praise as theft; 436 adds that the gold so earned goes to the courtesans.

424 quotes the poet's flattery of women, breasts like pots, teeth like pearls, peacock, Lakshmi of the lotus, as he coaxes them and worships their feet (அவர் தாடொழு). 436 quotes the flattery of patrons, kalpaka tree, cloud, Pari, made to end poverty (மிடிபோக). The same stock comparisons serve desire in one song and begging in the other, and 436 joins the two trades when the patron's gold goes to the women.

The Naladiyar's renunciant will not be moved by petty men who call eyes water-lilies, darting carp or spears (தெண்ணீர்க் குவளை பொருகயல் வேலென்று), having seen an eye is a scooped palm fruit. 437 lists the same likenings, deer, poison, carp, arrow, vel, sword, blue lily (கயல் மீனை ... வடிவேலை ... உற்பலத்தினை), then names the body an oozing filth and a bloated corpse (ஊதும் பிணம்). The song confesses being caught by the comparisons the quatrain sees through, and asks that the delusion clear (இப்ரமை தெளியாதோ).

The Naladiyar likens a harlot's love to a lamp: the light ends when the oil runs out, and her love ends when the hand is empty (கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). 438 lists the courtesans who for love of coin sell their breasts to many (காசாசையில் முலை பலர்க்கும் விற்பவர்) and the low-priced (விலைச்சிறுக்கிகள்). Both make money the whole measure of the love.

The Kural warns that the sweet words of bangled women who desire wealth, not love, bring harm (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும் ... இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்). 439 shows such women crying the price of their breasts in the street (முலை விலைகூறி), luring with deceitful play and snatching life (உயிரே பறிப்பவர்கள்), and asks whether they can be kin (உறவாமோ). The song's scene is the Kural's sale and harm made visible.

In the Naladiyar, to women without their companion the thunder of rain sounds like the funeral drum beaten in every direction (நெய்தல் அறைந்தன்ன). In 440 the roaring sea that bends and cries out (வளைந்து அரற்று கடல்) and the moon rising with poison torment the separated girl. Both turn a sound of nature into the separated woman's affliction; 440 then asks for mukti as the end of it.

The Kural names double-minded women, liquor and dice as the company of those whom Fortune has cast off (இருமனப் பெண்டிரும் கள்ளும் கவறும்). 442 gives the women a hundred thousand minds (நூறாயிர மனமுடை மாபாவிகள்) and calls itself the clown reviled by earth and sky who is wholly in their thrall. The Kural's two minds become the song's hundred thousand.

source_issues: Song 430: corrupt character in லு஡றிய (line 3), probably லூறிய ('oozing', of the serpent's poison).
Song 435: line 2 reads முமுடன், with a letter lost; probably முழுமூடன் or மூமூடன் ('utter fool').
Song 438: line 6 reads கின்ற்முடர் (probably கின்ற மூடர்) and line 18 தொணடர் (for தொண்டர்); neither is flagged.
Song 442: corrupt character in னு஡றாயிர (line 3), for நூறாயிர ('a hundred thousand').
